questions.question_text: Which of the following features is true of Huntington's disease?

options.text: Genetic defect located on long arm of chromosome 4
Results from an expanded CGG repeat

questions.explanation: 5 to 7% of deaths among patients with Huntington's resulted from suicide and nearly 25% of patients attempt suicide at least once. More than half of the suicides occurred in individuals who showed early signs of the illness but who had not been diagnosed, suggesting that suicide may occur more frequently in the early stages of the illness (Retrieved from http://www.ncbi.nl m.nih.gov/pubmed/6239910).

questions.question_text: In which of the following dementias one is likely to find better recognition memory than recall memory?
questions.explanation: HIV dementia is subcortical dementia. Recognition is better than recall in subcortical dementia while both are equally impaired in cortical dementia.

questions.question_text: A 42-year-old man has been complaining of troublesome motor activity for the last three years. He also has symptoms of irritability, anxiety, and low mood. He turns up an hour late for his medical appointment and shouts at the receptionist for not being punctual. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The age along with memory problems and psychiatric symptoms in the presence of motor problems suggest Huntington's chorea.

questions.question_text: The greatest risk factor for multi-infarct dementia is
questions.explanation: Vascular risk factors, such as type 2 diabetes, hypertension, obesity and dyslipidaemia often co-occur. Each of these factors has been associated with an increased risk of dementia, but it is uncertain which factor imposes the greatest risk. At midlife, the population attributable risk of dementia was highest for hypertension, up to 30% of cases of late-life dementia. Later in life diabetes appears to convey the highest risk of dementia. (Kloppenborg et al., 2008)(Retrieved from http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6239910)

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about hyperhomocysteinaemia is correct?

options.text: It is a risk factor for schizophrenia
It is a risk factor for autism
It is a risk factor for bipolar disorder
It is a risk factor for dementia
It is a risk factor for depression

correct_answer.text: It is a risk factor for dementia

correct_answers.text: It is a risk factor for dementia

questions.explanation: An increased plasma homocysteine level is a strong, independent risk factor for the development of dementia and Alzheimer's disease.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true for late onset schizophrenia?

options.text: There is usually a life long history of poor social and occupational functioning
It is seen more often in females than males
A strong family history is often noted
Response to treatment is much better than early onset schizophrenia

correct_answer.text: It is seen more often in females than males

correct_answers.text: It is seen more often in females than males

questions.explanation: Late-onset schizophrenia is seen more often in females than males. Gender distribution is estimated as 4 to 9 female predominance per male. Sensory impairments such as deafness is commonly associated. Compared to young onset schizophrenia, there is less often a strong family history in late onset schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: A 77-year-old man has developed Parkinson's disease. He starts sending his wife sexually abusive text messages and offensive comments, which is new and out of character. Which of the following medications is most likely to have caused this?
questions.explanation: L-dopa administration in Parkinson's disease can lead to increased levels of brain dopamine that may play a role in the development of hypomania and manic symptoms in such patients.

questions.question_text: What is the most common behavioural change observed in patients with Huntington's disease?
questions.explanation: The prevalence of behavioural problems is higher than expected in patients with Huntington's disease (Craufurd et al., 2001). The most common behavioral change observed in patients with Huntington's disease is a lack of initiative followed by poor judgement, blunting of affect, poor self-care, self-centeredness and inflexibility. Irritability, impulsivity and verbal outbursts are also reported ranging from 15 to 60% of cases. Ref: Craufurd D Thompson JC Snowden (2001); Behavioral change in Huntington's disease. Neuropsychiatry and behavioral neurology; 14: 219-226

questions.question_text: Deficits on tests of attention and visuospatial ability may be especially prominent in
questions.explanation: Although this feature may be seen in all types of dementia, neuropsychological studies imply that deficits on tests of attention, concentration and visuospatial dysfunction is seen more in Lewy body type of dementia.

questions.question_text: A 63-year-old lady with a mixed affective state also suffers from psoriasis. Which drug is most likely to worsen her skin condition?
questions.explanation: Some skin conditions such as psoriasis and acne can be aggravated by lithium therapy.

questions.question_text: A 74-year-old man presents with history of forgetfulness and some confusion at times. Which of the following factor delays the onset of dementia in this case?

options.text: Being a smoker in adult life

questions.explanation: Among many factors that have been studied with respect to predicting the onset of Alzheimer's, a cognitively, physically and socially active lifestyle in late life has been hypothesized to reduce the risk for Alzheimer's disease. Longer years of formal education has been shown to reduce the risk of conversion (MIRAGE study data). Perneczky, R et al., 'Education attenuates the effect of medial temporal lobe atrophy on cognitive function in Alzheimer's disease: the MIRAGE study,' Journal of Alzheimer's Disease: JAD 17, no. 4 (2009): 855-862.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following interventions is not recommended when managing delirium in the elderly?

options.text: Reduce the effects of sensory impediments
Preferably use low dose haloperidol for patients who require drug treatment
Preferably use benzodiazepines for patients who require drug treatment
Achieve optimal levels of environmental stimulation
Ensure the safety of all patients and their immediate surroundings

correct_answer.text: Preferably use benzodiazepines for patients who require drug treatment

correct_answers.text: Preferably use benzodiazepines for patients who require drug treatment

questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines used in delirium have the disadvantage of operating as potential aggravating factors in delirium, and elderly patients are at high risk of falls and disinhibition.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about neurotic disorders in the elderly is not true?

options.text: Obessional, dissociative and conversion disorders are less common
Males are predominantly affected than females
The estimated prevalence of neurotic disorders is between 1 -10%
Non specific anxiety symptoms, hypochondriacal and depressive symptoms predominate
Multiple factors may contribute to new neurotic symptoms in the elderly

correct_answer.text: Males are predominantly affected than females

correct_answers.text: Males are predominantly affected than females

questions.explanation: The estimated prevalence of neurotic disorders is between 1 -10% with a female predominance. Non-specific anxiety symptoms, Hypochondriacal and depressive symptoms predominate. Obsessional, phobic, Dissociative and conversion disorders are less common. There is an increase in referrals to psychiatry due to decreased acceptance of symptoms by the elderly. The most common ones are; physical illness, major life events, bereavement, social isolation, impaired self-care and insecure personality factors.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following neuroimaging techniques used when assessing dementia is helpful in studying white matter lesions and vascular lesions?
questions.explanation: MRI scan is helpful in identifying white matter lesions and vascular changes in the cortical and subcortical regions of the brain, which aids in the differential diagnosis of dementia. It is also helpful in identifying lesions in the posterior fossa of the brain.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old man has been diagnosed with Lewy body dementia. You are starting him on rivastigmine based on your consultant's suggestion. Which of the following side effect is most likely to happen?
questions.explanation: The most frequently reported adverse events with a higher rate in patients taking rivastigmine than placebo were nausea, vomiting and tremor.

questions.question_text: The most common psychiatric side effect of levo-dopa among the following is
questions.explanation: Up to 1/3rd of patients complain of psychiatric side effects when taking levodopa therapy. Nearly 30% of those taking levodopa complain of nightmares and vivid dreams. This is followed by 7% with night terrors, 5% with delirium and 3% with delusional disorder.

questions.question_text: The neurotransmitters that are most often implicated in the pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease are
questions.explanation: The neurotransmitters that are most often implicated in the pathophysiological condition of Alzheimer's disease are Acetylcholine and norepinephrine, both of which are hypothesized to be hypoactive in Alzheimer's disease.

questions.question_text: The personality disorder that is most prevalent after 60 years of age is
questions.explanation: A British study (Cohen, 1994) suggested that older subjects were significantly less likely than younger subjects to have any PD (6.6% vs. 10.5%; OR 0.42). This difference was almost entirely attributable to a threefold higher prevalence of dramatic PDs (Cluster B) in the younger cohorts. The largest differences were in Antisocial PD and Histrionic PD. This study found that the highest prevalence of a PD in elderly was for Obsessive-Compulsive PD (DSM-III) at a rate of 3.3%.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is contraindicated in the elderly with psychosis and cognitive impairment?
questions.explanation: Having reviewed the literature on the use of Olanzapine and Risperidone for the behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia, the committee on safety of medicines concluded that each was associated with at least two-fold increase in the risk of stroke and should, therefore, be no longer used in dementia (Duff 2004)

questions.question_text: Older people with dementia often do not tolerate drugs as well as a healthy older person. Which of the following is contraindicated in patients with dementia?
questions.explanation: The chairman of the CSM concluded that risperidone and olanzapine are associated with at least a two-fold increase in the risk of stroke and, therefore, should no longer be used in dementia (Duff, 2004). Herrmann et al. (2004), however, found no difference in the risk of stroke between risperidone and olanzapine compared with typical neuroleptics used in the treatment of behavioural problems in those with dementia (n=11400). Others have subsequently commented on the potential detrimental effects of such a blanket ban (Mowat et al, 2004 )(Karim and Byrne, Treatment of psychosis in elderly people | BJPsych Advances. (2005). Retrieved from http://apt.rcpsych.o rg/content/11/4/286). Promazine has a relatively good side effect profile and so is suitable for the elderly. It is not effective for schizophrenia (Maudsley Guidelines. 2007).

questions.question_text: Compared to other subtypes, paranoid subtype of schizophrenia is more often associated with which of the following features?
questions.explanation: Features such as poorer premorbid function, poorer psychosocial recovery, worse cognitive deficits and earlier age of onset are associated with hebephrenic or disorganized schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Factors associated with good prognosis in Alzheimer's disease include
questions.explanation: Later onset, female gender, an absence of behavioural symptoms, and lack of depressive episodes suggest better prognosis in Alzheimer's disease.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a good prognostic factor in old age depression?

options.text: Severe life events during follow up period

questions.explanation: Good prognostic factors include 1.Onset less than 70 years of age 2.a shorter duration of illness 3.Absence of physical illness 4.Good previous adjustment 5.Good previous recovery.

questions.question_text: The response to antidepressants is expected to be generally poor in
questions.explanation: Alexopoulos et al. (1997) proposed that cerebral ischaemic damage to the frontal-subcortical circuits could predispose, precipitate and perpetuate late-onset depression. Simpson et al. studied the association between subcortical disease and antidepressant response in late-life depression, concluding that a poor response could be expected in patients with vascular depression.

questions.question_text: A 76-year-old woman presents to her GP upon her daughter's insistence. She exhibits features of late paraphrenia. Which of the following types of delusions is most likely to be seen?
questions.explanation: Late paraphrenia is the most common form of psychosis in old age. Persecutory delusions are the most common symptoms of late paraphrenia and tend to relate to common themes such as neighbours spying. Auditory hallucinations occur in approximately 75% of cases.

questions.question_text: The most prevalent anxiety disorders among older adults is;
questions.explanation: In people over age 65, anxiety disorders are the most prevalent psychiatric disorders, excluding the dementias. The most prevalent anxiety disorder among older adults is phobic disorder and the least common in this age group is the panic disorder. The anxiety disorders are more prevalent in women than in men across all age groups.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man admitted to a neurology unit has an unsteady gait and repeated falls. This is most likely to be associated with
questions.explanation: Risk factors for falling in an elderly patient could be classified as either intrinsic (e.g., lower extremity weakness, poor grip strength, balance disorders, functional and cognitive impairment, visual deficits) or extrinsic (e.g., polypharmacy (i.e., four or more prescription medications) and environmental factors such as poor lighting, loose carpets, and lack of bathroom safety equipment). A meta-analysis that studied the relationship of falls and medications, which included studies that examined both multiple and single risk factors, found a significantly increased risk from psychotropic medication (odds ratio (OR) 1.7), Class 1a antiarrhythmic medications (OR 1.6), digoxin (OR 1.2), and diuretics (OR 1.1). Leipzig RM, Cumming RG, Tinetti ME. Drugs and falls in older people: A systematic review and meta-analysis: I. Psychotropic drugs. J Am Geriatr Soc 1999;47:30-39.

questions.question_text: According to NINCD-ADRDA criteria, which of the following is NOT a criterion required to diagnose probable Alzheimer's disease?

options.text: Presence of cerebral atrophy in neuroimaging studies
No disturbance in level of consciousness
Absence of systemic diseases or other brain diseases that could explain the cognitive changes
Cognitive deficit is seen in more than one domain

correct_answer.text: Presence of cerebral atrophy in neuroimaging studies

correct_answers.text: Presence of cerebral atrophy in neuroimaging studies

questions.explanation: Cognitive deficits must be seen in 2 or more domains. The absence of loss of consciousness, presence of cerebral atrophy, an appropriate age of onset and absence of other systemic diseases to explain cognitive deficits support the diagnosis of probable AD.

questions.question_text: Compared with early onset depression, people with late-onset depression tend to present more often with symptoms of
questions.explanation: Late onset depression is associated more with cognitive impairment, anhedonia, psychomotor changes (Hickie et al. 2001) and weight loss (Janssen Et Al 2006) severe life stress (Vandenberg et al. 2001). Severe psychomotor retardation or agitation occurs in up to 30% of depressed elderly patients. Cognitive impairment has been detected in 70% of cases. The frequency and severity of life events (physical illness, loss of a spouse) may be greater in later life than in the general population.(Hughes Et Al 1988). Grace and O'Briens findings that bereavement life events were more common in those with early onset depression suggest that older people may be better able to cope with bereavements even though they are at increased risk of experiencing them.

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old man with Parkinson's disease develops psychosis unrelated to levodopa use. Choose the best antipsychotic for his treatment.
questions.explanation: Eight open-label studies have assessed quetiapine use in 191 patients with psychosis and Parkinson's disease, with improvement in psychosis recorded in 152 (80%). In addition to the open-label studies, there have been two single-blind, randomized trials comparing quetiapine and clozapine. These studies suggest that quetiapine has similar efficacy to clozapine in controlling psychosis.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best indicates the status of estrogen treatment in postmenopausal women with Alzheimer's disease?

options.text: RCTs find no improvement in the Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores
RCTs find an improvement in MMSE scores that is sustained for at least one year
No RCTs have been conducted to examine the effects of estrogen in this clinical group
RCTs consistently show beneficial effects on activities of daily living
RCTs find small short-term improvements in MMSE scores that do not translate to clinical benefit

correct_answer.text: RCTs find small short-term improvements in MMSE scores that do not translate to clinical benefit

correct_answers.text: RCTs find small short-term improvements in MMSE scores that do not translate to clinical benefit

questions.explanation: A Cochrane systematic review identified five RCTs that included 210 postmenopausal women with Alzheimer disease. "The reviewers looked at various outcomes (such as MMSE, memory, concentration, and cognitive function) after treatment with different types of estrogen, at different doses, delivered by different routes and for different durations. Meta-analyses showed that there was a limited positive effect from low-dose conjugated equine estrogens (0.625 mg once a day) but not from a higher dose (1.25 mg of conjugated equine estrogens once a day) on the MMSE after two months, but the effect disappeared after three, six, and 12 months of treatment. This effect was small and not clinically relevant." (http://journa ls.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371/journal.pmed.0020031)

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a neurobiological feature of normal ageing process?

options.text: Reduction in the weight of the brain
Loss of nerve cells in the hippocampus
Reduction in cerebral blood flow in the frontal lobe

questions.explanation: There is a reduction in the weight and volume of the brain by 5% between ages 30 and 70, by 10% by the age of 80, and by 20% by the age of 90. There is a loss of nerve cells in the cortex, hippocampus, substantia nigra and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum. There may also be a reduction in the dendritic processes.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements concerning pharmacokinetics in the elderly is true?

options.text: Renal blood flow reduces with age even in those with normal physical health
Serum creatinine measurement is the most accurate way of measuring renal function
Total gastrointestinal drug absorption is reduced in the elderly
25% of adult renal function is lost by 80 years

correct_answer.text: Renal blood flow reduces with age even in those with normal physical health

correct_answers.text: Renal blood flow reduces with age even in those with normal physical health

questions.explanation: Though GI absorption becomes slower, it does not get reduced quantitatively. Creatinine measurements can yield spurious results; hence GFR formulas must be used to correct for age and other variables. Gastric pH increases with age (less acidic). Nearly 40% renal function is lost by the age 80. The average decline is around 10mL/min/1.73m2 per decade after age 30. This takes an adult GFR from 130mL/min/1.73m2 to a value of 80mL/min/1.73m2 when the age is 80 (The Baltimore Longitudinal Study). Kidney mass has been reported to be substantially reduced in old age, by approximately 20 to 25% between the age of 30 and 80 years. Renal blood flow reduces with age even in those with normal health. Renal blood flow decreases by about 10% per decade after the age of 20. By age 80, RBF may be 600ml/min as compared to 1200ml/min in young adults. Schrier, RW. Diseases of the Kidney and Urinary Tract: Clinicopathologic Foundations of Medicine. Lippincott -Wilkins, 2007 Pg 301.

questions.question_text: A70 year old lady has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's dementia recently. What is the risk of same illness for her sister provided there is no other family history of Alzheimer's dementia?

options.text: Risk will be three times higher

correct_answer.text: Risk will be three times higher

correct_answers.text: Risk will be three times higher

questions.explanation: The actual predicted risk of developing Alzheimer's disease in the first-degree relatives of probands with Alzheimer's disease is 15 -19%, compared with 5% in controls. Thus, the risk to the first-degree relatives of patients with Alzheimer's disease who developed the disorder at any time up to the age of 85 years is increased some 3 - 4 times relative to the risk in controls. This would seem to translate to a risk of developing Alzheimer's disease of between one in five and one in six. Liddell et al. (2001) Genetic risk of Alzheimer's disease: advising relatives. The British Journal of Psychiatry, 178, 7 -11.

questions.question_text: You are seeing a 77-year-old man with late onset psychosis. He has a history of falls due to postural hypotension. Which drug is most likely to cause orthostatic hypotension?
questions.explanation: Risperidone and Clozapine are two drugs, which have a greater risk of causing severe postural hypotension. The suggested drugs are amisulpride, aripiprazole, haloperidol and sulpiride.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidementia drugs produces significant improvements in delusions and hallucinations seen in patients with Lewy Body dementia?
questions.explanation: A large multicenter, double-blind trial comparing Rivastigmine with placebo in patients with LBD showed significant improvements in delusions and hallucinations (Mc Keith et al. 2000). Cholinesterase inhibitors are not yet licensed for the treatment of LBD in UK but substantial provisional evidence suggest that ACHEIs are effective in some LBD cases for improvement in cognitive functions and also in treating neuropsychiatric features such as apathy, agitation and psychosis.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old gentleman suffers from Parkinson's disease and is also currently depressed. His wife says he has been sending her sexually explicit texts and also accused her of having an affair. This is a new type of behaviour and is out of keeping with his previous pattern of behaviour when depressed. Which drug is most likely to account for this presentation?
questions.explanation: Ropinirole can be used by itself or in conjunction with levodopa to treat Parkinson's disease, and is particularly useful in people for whom levodopa alone is no longer providing adequate control of symptom. Ropinirole works by stimulating these same receptor sites. This produces the same effects as dopamine and acts as a dopamine substitute. Increased sex drive (libido) and excessive interest or involvement in sexual activity (hypersexuality) is uncommon but possible side effect of this medication (Retrieved from http://www.netdoctor.co.uk/seniors-health/medicines/requip.html).

questions.question_text: An elderly lady reports smelling of gas passed through the walls and thought her neighbours are trying to poison her. She has contacted the police on a number of occasions over last 3 months claiming that neighbours are spying on her. The most likely diagnosis is;
questions.explanation: Late-onset schizophrenia is characterized by paranoid delusions and hallucinations. The patients usually complain of partition delusions as described above and may harbour persecutory delusions against neighbours. Social isolation and sensory deprivation are significant contributory factors for psychosis in the elderly. Confusingly, ICD-10 includes paraphrenia along with paranoid schizophrenia, and also includes the term paraphrenia with delusional disorders. In the presence of hallucinations, schizophrenia is the most appropriate diagnosis.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a recognized neuroimaging finding in late-onset depression?

options.text: Reduction in grey matter volume in frontal and temporal lobes
Reduction in the volume of the caudate nucleus

questions.explanation: Ventricles appear enlarged, not shrunk, in geriatric depression.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about learning and memory in the elderly is not true?

options.text: Complete learning of new materials still occurs
IQ remains stable until approximately 70 years of age
The elderly take longer than young persons to learn new material

questions.explanation: Cognitive profile changes distinctly with the age of an individual. IQ peaks at 25 years, plateaus until 60 -70 and then declines. Simple recall becomes difficult, and memory encoding ability diminishes. Although the elderly take longer than younger persons to learn new material, complete learning of new material still occurs. Working memory shows a gradual decline in capacity and it is worse with increased complexity of tasks and increased memory load. Long-term memory declines. However, remote events of personal significance may be recalled with great clarity. Older people also maintain their verbal abilities, and there is a possible drop in verbal IQ, performance IQ and problem-solving abilities after the age of 80.

questions.question_text: Which classes of antidepressants are used as first-line treatments for late-onset depression?
questions.explanation: SSRIs are often used as the first line treatment for late-onset depression due to their lower propensity to cause side effects and relative safety in overdose.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a type of prion disease?
questions.explanation: Prion protein is a normal brain protein, whose function is unknown. Prion related diseases occur when the protein undergoes changes, which renders it insoluble. The diseases caused by prions are spongiform encephalopathies, which are transmissible dementias. There are four forms of the disease in humans, all of which are rare. These are; 1. Kuru 2. Creutzfeldt -Jakob Disease 3.Fatal familial insomnia 4. Gerstmann Straussler syndrome.

questions.question_text: An important feature differentiating vascular dementia from Alzheimer's disease is
questions.explanation: The Hachinski Ischaemic Score (HIS) "represents a brief clinical tool helpful in the "bedside" differentiation of the commonest dementia types, Dementia of Alzheimer's Type (DAT) and Vascular Dementia (VaD). It's utility has been validated by meta-analysis in pathologically verified patients with dementia. A cut-off score = 4 for DAT and = 7 for VaD has a sensitivity of 89% and a specificity of 89% (Moroney 1997). It is not useful in determinations between mixed dementia and other dementia types. HIS items distinguishing VaD from DAT were stepwise deterioration (odds ratio (OR), 6.06), fluctuating course (OR, 7.60), hypertension (OR, 4.30), history of stroke (OR, 4.30) and focal neurological symptoms (OR, 4.40)." (excerpt from Moroney, J.T., Meta-analysis of the Hachinski Ischaemic Score in pathologically verified dementias. Neurology, 49, 1096 - 1105.).

questions.question_text: The type of dementia seen in patients with Parkinson's disease is
questions.explanation: Subcortical pattern of dementia is seen in Parkinson's disease dementia.

questions.question_text: Features suggestive of pseudodementia include all except

options.text: The patients often complain about poor memory
Assessment of cognitive function often results in "Don't Know" answers
There is often a past history of depression or an identifiable precipitant

questions.explanation: With respect to pseudodementia, the onset can be dated with some precision while symptoms are of shorter duration before medical help is sought. There may be a more rapid progression of symptoms after onset than seen with organic dementia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with regard to the pharmacokinetics of psychotropics in the elderly?

options.text: The volume of distribution of fat soluble drugs is reduced
Serum creatinine accurately reflects renal function
By the age of 80, nearly 25% of renal function is lost
The amount of drug absorbed after oral intake is reduced
The rate of absorption of drugs is slower

correct_answer.text: The rate of absorption of drugs is slower

correct_answers.text: The rate of absorption of drugs is slower

questions.explanation: The rate of absorption is slower but nearly equal absorption of oral administered drugs. Absorption is not greatly affected. GI blood flow is diminished. Gastric pH is increased as acidity drops. Decreases in renal blood flow have been approximated at 10% per decade beginning after the fourth decade - leads to reduced creatinine clearance and GFR. A larger volume of distribution and longer half-life of lipophilic chemicals noted because of their increased sequestration in fat e.g.; Benzodiazepines are excreted more slowly in elderly.

questions.question_text: Picks disease is characterised by all except

options.text: There is prominent atrophy of the white matter with relative sparing of the grey matter
It is caused by Autosomal dominant mutation in the Tau gene (chromosome 17) with complete penetration
The onset is usually between 45 -65 years
There is positive family history in 50% of cases
Knife blade atrophy on CT/MRI scan is commonly seen in most cases

correct_answer.text: There is prominent atrophy of the white matter with relative sparing of the grey matter

correct_answers.text: There is prominent atrophy of the white matter with relative sparing of the grey matter

questions.explanation: In Pick's Disease, CT/MRI brain reveals bilateral symmetrical abnormalities of the frontal and temporal lobes. A milder generalised atrophy but a marked atrophy of frontal and temporal lobes with sparing of the posterior third of the superior temporal gyrus produces the so-called called Knife blade atro phy. Both grey and white matter is equally affected with blurring of the boundary.

questions.question_text: Which of the following features is not related to the biological changes seen with normal aging process?

options.text: Progressive hearing loss particularly at the high frequencies
Decrease in cardiac output and stroke volume

questions.explanation: Changes in bodily function during old age includes a decrease in cardiac output and stroke volume, a decrease in glomerular filtration rate, a reduction in cerebral blood flow and oxygenation, decreased vital capacity in the lungs, decrease in melatonin, thickening of the optic lens in association with an inability to accommodate and progressive hearing loss particularly at the high frequencies.

questions.question_text: Mrs. Y is an 83-year-old lady whose sister has been diagnosed with early Alzheimer's disease. She is worried that she may develop the same condition. What is her risk compared to a person who lacks such a family history?
questions.explanation: An actual predicted risk of developing Alzheimer's disease in the first-degree relatives of probands with Alzheimer's disease is 15 -19%, compared with 5% in controls. Thus, the risk to the first-degree relatives of patients with Alzheimer's disease who developed the disorder at any time up to the age of 85 years is increased some 3 - 4 times relative to the risk in controls (Retrieved from http://bjp.rcpsych.org/content/178/1/7).

questions.question_text: Which of the following can be used as a test of executive functioning in an older person with schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: The tower of Hanoi is frequently used in psychological research on problem solving and executive functions. It is also a test used by neuropsychologists trying to evaluate frontal lobe deficits. The tower of Hanoi is a mathematical puzzle with three rods and a number of disks of different sizes which can slide onto any rod.

questions.question_text: Ginkgo is a popular herbal remedy for memory enhancement. Patients treated for which of the following conditions should strictly avoid Ginkgo?

options.text: Treated for atrial fibrillation with warfarin
Treated for dental pain with ibuprofen
Treated for bacterial pharyngitis with amoxicillin
Treated for Paget's disease with alendronate

correct_answer.text: Treated for atrial fibrillation with warfarin

correct_answers.text: Treated for atrial fibrillation with warfarin

questions.explanation: Ginkgolide B present in Ginkgo inhibits platelet activating factor by displacing it from its binding sites. This antiplatelet activity leads to interaction with warfarin and may cause fatal spontaneous cerebral bleeds.

questions.question_text: In dementia with Lewy bodies, visual hallucinations have been reported in;
questions.explanation: In Lewy body dementia, at least 60 to 80% cases report visual or auditory hallucinations. Mild spontaneous extra pyramidal features (70% of cases) is also common along with repeated unexplained falls or transient clouding or loss of consciousness and increased sensitivity to neuroleptics (60% of cases).

questions.question_text: Hachinski score is a way of looking into risk factors for
questions.explanation: The Hachinski Ischaemic Score (HIS) represents a brief clinical tool helpful in the "bedside" differentiation of the commonest dementia types, Dementia of Alzheimer's Type (DAT) and Vascular Dementia (VaD). It's utility has been validated by meta-analysis in pathologically verified patients with dementia.

questions.question_text: In Parkinson's related psychosis, hallucinations in which sensory modality is common?
questions.explanation: Parkinson's related psychosis is mostly related to antiparkinsonian drugs. Both dopaminergic/anticholinergic medications are implicated. Hallucinations are common, seen in 20% of cases - especially visual modality, delusions 3 -30%. Low-dose (less than 100 mg/day) clozapine can improve psychosis without worsening parkinsonism. Quetiapine can also be used.

questions.question_text: A characteristic feature in diagnosis of Lewy body dementia is
questions.explanation: Visual hallucinations can be present in more than 80% of patients with LBD.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is classified as a 'behavioural symptom' seen in Alzheimer's Dementia?
questions.explanation: In patients with Alzheimer's, behavioural symptoms would include wandering, aggression, anger outbursts, sexual disinhibition, incontinence, excessive eating and searching behaviour. Psychiatric symptoms include delusions (15%), auditory and visual hallucinations (10 -15%), and depression requiring treatment in 20% of patients.
